analysis.one_liner: Required health plans to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care after a mastectomy and 24 hours after lymph node surgery.
analysis.headline: A bill guaranteeing 48 hours of hospital coverage after a mastectomy drew 220 House cosponsors — 194 Democrats and 25 Republicans — but never received a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped health insurers from limiting hospital stays after breast cancer surgery to less than 48 hours after a mastectomy or 24 hours after a lymph node dissection, unless the woman and her doctor agreed to an earlier discharge. It also barred insurers from paying women to leave early, penalizing doctors who let patients stay, or dropping women from coverage to dodge the rule. It applied to both employer plans and individual insurance, and it did not override state laws that were already at least as strong.
analysis.who_benefits: Women with health insurance undergoing mastectomy or lymph node dissection for breast cancer. They would no longer face coverage rules pushing them out of the hospital within hours of major surgery, and their doctors would not need advance permission from the insurer to order a stay covered by the minimum.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and insurers from covering less than 48 hours in the hospital after a mastectomy or less than 24 hours after a lymph node dissection.

Lets a woman leave earlier only if her attending doctor decides it in consultation with her — the decision stays with the patient and physician, not the insurer, and plans may not require prior authorization for the minimum stay.

Bars insurers from offering women cash rebates to accept less than the minimum stay, from penalizing doctors who follow the rule, and from denying or dropping a woman's coverage just to avoid the requirement.
Applies the same protections to individual-market insurance, and leaves stronger state laws in place rather than preempting them.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and workers who fund employer health plans, through the added cost of covering longer hospital stays after breast cancer surgery. The bill leaves insurers free to keep setting deductibles and cost-sharing and to negotiate reimbursement levels with providers.

drawbacks.text: A federal minimum-stay mandate raises claims costs for insurers and self-insured employer plans, which flow into premiums — a real cost, though targeted to one category of surgery.

Critics of benefit mandates argue that one-size-fits-all federal rules substitute Washington's judgment for the case-by-case medical judgment the bill itself tries to protect; the bill answers this by allowing earlier discharge when the doctor and patient agree, but it still sets a federal floor on covered care.
The bill does not require any woman to stay in the hospital, but plans that do not cover hospital stays for these procedures at all are exempt, and the mandate does nothing for uninsured women.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a specific group — roughly the tens of thousands of women each year having breast cancer surgery — and the bill is carefully drawn: it keeps discharge decisions with the doctor and patient, allows earlier discharge by agreement, preserves cost-sharing and provider reimbursement negotiations, and defers to stronger state laws. The cost is higher premiums spread across everyone with coverage. The design is narrow and its protections direct; the main honest objection is philosophical, over federal mandates on private insurance generally.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then sent to subcommittees in each, and neither ever brought it up before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, joined by 100 original cosponsors from both parties.

The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee on the day of introduction, and within a month was sent to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations.
The bill eventually drew 220 cosponsors — 194 Democrats, 25 Republicans, and 1 Independent — close to half the House.
No committee or subcommittee reported the bill, no floor vote ever occurred, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans that limited post-surgery hospital stays kept operating under no federal floor, saving the cost of longer covered stays. Cosponsors also kept the credit of supporting a popular bill that never had to face a recorded vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and plans that capped stays

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic but not exclusively: 194 of 211 House Democrats cosponsored alongside 25 of 223 Republicans and the chamber's Independent, giving the bill 220 cosponsors of 435 members — yet the Republican-controlled committees never acted on it.

industries.note: Insurers at the time limited post-mastectomy hospital stays to control costs, sometimes with 'drive-through' discharges; the bill would have forced them to cover a 48-hour minimum and barred workarounds like rebates to women who left early or penalties on doctors. The insurer savings from short stays came at the expense of women recovering from major surgery.

ERISA plans would bear somewhat higher claims costs for longer covered stays, but the bill keeps cost-sharing and reimbursement negotiation intact and applies only to plans that cover these procedures at all.
Guaranteed minimum stays would mean more inpatient reimbursement for surgical care, and here the hospitals' interest ran with the patients' recovery rather than against it.
